fathers/evagrius-ponticus/summary: Greek deacon from Pontus (c. 345–399), disciple of the Cappadocians and of the Egyptian monks, who systematised desert spirituality — the eight evil thoughts, apatheia, pure prayer — and was posthumously condemned as an Origenist, yet shaped monastic theology East and West.
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/story:
Evagrius was born around 345 at Ibora in Pontus, the son of a country bishop (chorepiscopus). Basil of Caesarea ordained him reader, and Gregory of Nazianzus made him deacon; he served Gregory in Constantinople in 379–381, where he became a celebrated preacher and controversialist against the Arians during the period of the Council of Constantinople. An infatuation with a married noblewoman, a warning dream and a sudden flight brought him in 382 to Jerusalem, where Melania the Elder and Rufinus received him in their monastery on the Mount of Olives. After a severe illness he took the monastic habit at Melania’s urging.

In 383 he went to Egypt, spending two years at Nitria and then fourteen in the more remote Kellia, living by copying manuscripts. He became a disciple of Macarius the Great and Macarius of Alexandria, and the centre of a circle of educated monks that included Palladius and the ‘Tall Brothers’. He died at Epiphany 399, on the eve of the Origenist controversy that would scatter his disciples.

Evagrius’s genius was to give the oral wisdom of the desert a precise, almost technical structure. In the Praktikos he describes eight ‘thoughts’ (logismoi) through which demons attack the monk — gluttony, fornication, avarice, sadness, anger, acedia (listless restlessness, ‘the noonday demon’), vainglory and pride — and their remedies. The goal of the ascetic life (praktike) is apatheia, a calm freedom from passion, whose offspring is love; beyond it lie natural contemplation (physike) and finally ‘theology’, the imageless knowledge of the Trinity in pure prayer. His Chapters on Prayer, long transmitted under the name of Nilus of Ancyra, contain the famous line that the theologian is the one who prays truly.

His speculative works, especially the Kephalaia Gnostika, set this ascent within an Origenist cosmology: rational minds (noes) originally united with God fell away into bodies and will be restored. These ideas were attacked in the Origenist controversies and condemned, together with Origen and Didymus, in the anathemas associated with the Council of Constantinople in 553. Many of his Greek works were therefore lost or survived under other names, while the full Kephalaia Gnostika survives only in Syriac, in a censored version and a more radical one discovered by Antoine Guillaumont in 1958.

Condemnation did not end his influence. Cassian carried the eight thoughts to Gaul, from which Gregory the Great reshaped them into the seven deadly sins. Maximus the Confessor and the Byzantine hesychasts used his ascetic teaching, and the Philokalia (1782) includes his texts under Nilus’s name. In the Syriac churches, especially the Church of the East, he was honoured as ‘the blessed Evagrius’ and shaped writers such as Isaac of Nineveh.
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/roots/0/text: Origen’s cosmology and exegesis, mediated through the Cappadocians and Didymus the Blind, supply the framework of his speculative theology.
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/roots/1/text: Apatheia and the analysis of the passions as judgements and impulses draw on Stoic moral psychology, though Evagrius makes apatheia the doorway to love, not an end in itself.
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/roots/2/text: He uses Plato’s tripartite soul (rational, irascible, concupiscible) to classify the thoughts, and a Platonist ascent from the sensible to the intelligible.
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/roots/3/text: His teaching systematises what he learnt from the two Macarii and the oral tradition of Nitria and Kellia.
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/roots/4/text: His Antirrhetikos supplies biblical verses to answer each demonic thought, following Christ’s use of Scripture in the temptations; he wrote scholia on the Psalms, Proverbs and Ecclesiastes.
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/keyTeachings/0: The eight evil thoughts (logismoi) and the demons who exploit them, with acedia as the most oppressive
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/keyTeachings/1: Apatheia (dispassion) as the health of the soul, giving birth to agape
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/keyTeachings/2: The three stages: praktike (ascetic practice), physike (natural contemplation), theologia (knowledge of the Trinity)
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/keyTeachings/3: Pure, imageless prayer as the highest activity of the mind
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/keyTeachings/4: ‘Antirrhetic’ prayer: answering each temptation with a verse of Scripture
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/keyTeachings/5: Speculative Origenism: the pre-existence and fall of minds and their final restoration
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/works/0/note: One hundred chapters on the ascetic life and the eight thoughts; the first part of a trilogy with the Gnostikos and Kephalaia Gnostika.
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/works/1/note: 153 chapters on pure prayer, long transmitted under the name of Nilus of Ancyra and included in the Philokalia.
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/works/2/note: Six ‘centuries’ of speculative chapters, surviving complete only in Syriac; the main basis for his condemnation.
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/works/3/note: Biblical texts to counter the eight thoughts; survives in Syriac and Armenian.
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/works/4/title: On the Eight Thoughts; To Monks; To a Virgin
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/works/4/note: Shorter ascetic works and sentences, some preserved under Nilus’s name.
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/works/5/title: Letters, including the Great Letter (to Melania)
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/works/5/note: A Syriac collection of some sixty letters, including a summary of his cosmology.
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/doctrineContri: Gave Christian spirituality its first systematic map of the passions, stages of the spiritual life and contemplative prayer.
His eight thoughts became, through Cassian and Gregory the Great, the Western list of seven deadly sins.
A detailed demonology in which demons act on the mind through thoughts and memories rather than primarily through external apparitions.
His Origenist hope of the restoration of minds was condemned in 553 and remains a reference point in debates about universalism (apokatastasis).
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/laterInfluence: John Cassian transmitted his ascetic teaching to the Latin West without naming him; Gregory the Great reshaped the eight thoughts into seven capital sins.
Maximus the Confessor corrected his cosmology while adopting his ascetic and contemplative framework; the Philokalia carries his texts under Nilus’s name.
Widely translated into Syriac; foundational for the mystical writers of the Church of the East (Isaac of Nineveh, John of Dalyatha) and for Syriac Orthodox writers such as Philoxenus of Mabbug.
Guillaumont’s rediscovery of the unexpurgated Kephalaia Gnostika (1958) prompted a revival of study; his analysis of acedia and ‘thoughts’ has been compared with cognitive psychology.
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/reception/0/te: Condemned with Origen in 553 and not venerated as a saint, yet his ascetic teaching is read, often under Nilus’s name, in the Philokalia.
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/reception/1/te: Honoured as a great teacher of the monastic life; his works were central to East Syriac mysticism.
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/reception/2/tr: Syriac Orthodox and other Oriental Orthodox
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/reception/2/te: Read in Syriac translation and used by ascetic authors, with some reserve about his speculative teaching.
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/reception/3/te: Not venerated, but recognised as a principal source of Cassian and of the seven deadly sins; widely studied since the twentieth century.
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/reception/4/te: Little known before the twentieth century; now read as a spiritual and psychological classic in ecumenical spirituality.
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/controversies/: Posthumous condemnation as an Origenist: the fifteen anathemas against Origenist doctrines, associated with the Council of Constantinople (553), target views found in the Kephalaia Gnostika
How far his ascetic teaching depends on his speculative cosmology, and whether the two can be separated
The Origenist controversy of 399–400, when Theophilus of Alexandria expelled the Tall Brothers and other Evagrian monks from Nitria
fathers/evagrius-ponticus/quote/text: If you are a theologian you will pray truly, and if you pray truly you are a theologian.
fathers/jerome/summary: Dalmatian-born scholar and monk (c. 347–420) who learnt Hebrew, translated most of the Bible afresh into Latin (the core of the Vulgate), wrote commentaries on nearly every book of Scripture and fought bitter controversies on asceticism, Origen and grace from his monastery in Bethlehem.
fathers/jerome/story:
Jerome (Eusebius Hieronymus) was born at Stridon, a town on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia whose site is unknown; his birth date is disputed, with c. 347 the most widely accepted. He studied in Rome under the grammarian Aelius Donatus, acquiring a lifelong love of Cicero, Virgil and the classical style, and was baptised there around 366. After time at Trier and in an ascetic circle at Aquileia, he travelled east around 374. At Antioch he had his famous dream in which Christ the Judge accused him: ‘You are a Ciceronian, not a Christian’ (Letter 22.30).

He spent two or three years as a hermit in the desert of Chalcis in Syria, where he began learning Hebrew from a converted Jew. Ordained priest at Antioch by Paulinus, he went to Constantinople (c. 380–381), heard Gregory of Nazianzus and began translating Origen and Eusebius’s Chronicle. From 382 to 385 he was in Rome as secretary to Pope Damasus, who commissioned him to revise the Old Latin Gospels against the Greek. He became spiritual director to a circle of aristocratic women — Marcella, Paula and her daughters Blesilla and Eustochium — but his abrasive ascetic propaganda and the death of Blesilla made enemies, and after Damasus died he left Rome under a cloud.

In 386 Jerome and Paula settled at Bethlehem, founding monasteries for men and women and a hostel for pilgrims. There, using Origen’s Hexapla at Caesarea and the help of Jewish teachers, he produced a new Latin translation of the Hebrew Old Testament (c. 390–405). His principle of the ‘Hebrew truth’ (hebraica veritas) led him to set apart the books found only in the Greek Septuagint — the later ‘Apocrypha’ or deuterocanonical books — as useful for edification but not for establishing doctrine (Prologus Galeatus). Augustine worried that departing from the Septuagint would unsettle congregations; in one African town, a new rendering of Jonah’s plant caused a near riot.

Jerome was a formidable controversialist. Against Helvidius (383) he defended Mary’s perpetual virginity; Against Jovinian (393) argued that virginity is superior to marriage in terms that embarrassed even his friends; Against Vigilantius (406) defended the cult of relics and martyrs. Having once translated and praised Origen, he turned against him in the Origenist controversy and broke violently with his old friend Rufinus. Late in life he wrote against Pelagius (415). He also produced On Illustrious Men (392–393), the first Christian literary history, and a vast correspondence. He died at Bethlehem on 30 September 419 or 420.

His translation, combined with revised Old Latin books, became the ‘Vulgate’, the Bible of the Latin West for a thousand years; the Council of Trent declared it ‘authentic’ in 1546. Medieval art portrayed him as a cardinal in his study with a lion. For Erasmus, who edited his works in 1516, he was the model of the Christian scholar; for the Reformers, his distinction between the Hebrew canon and the other books supplied an ancient precedent for the Protestant Old Testament.
fathers/jerome/roots/0/text: Trained by Donatus in grammar and rhetoric; Cicero and Virgil shaped his style even after his dream, and he defended the use of pagan learning (Letter 70).
fathers/jerome/roots/1/text: He learnt Hebrew as an adult and made the Hebrew text, not the Septuagint, the basis of his Old Testament.
fathers/jerome/roots/2/text: He consulted Jewish teachers (such as Bar Hanina) and used Jewish traditions of interpretation, recorded in his Hebrew Questions on Genesis — rare among Latin Fathers.
fathers/jerome/roots/3/text: Origen was his exegetical model: he used the Hexapla and translated dozens of Origen’s homilies before turning against his doctrines; he heard Gregory of Nazianzus and Didymus the Blind.
fathers/jerome/roots/4/text: Inspired by Egyptian and Syrian ascetics, he wrote lives of the hermits Paul, Malchus and Hilarion and translated the Pachomian Rule.
fathers/jerome/keyTeachings/0: The ‘Hebrew truth’: Old Testament translation should be made from the Hebrew original
fathers/jerome/keyTeachings/1: A distinction between canonical books and ecclesiastical books read for edification (the later ‘Apocrypha’)
fathers/jerome/keyTeachings/2: Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ
fathers/jerome/keyTeachings/3: The perpetual virginity of Mary, with the ‘brothers of the Lord’ explained as cousins
fathers/jerome/keyTeachings/4: The superiority of virginity and ascetic renunciation over marriage
fathers/jerome/keyTeachings/5: Veneration of martyrs’ relics as honour to God, not worship of creatures
fathers/jerome/works/0/note: Revised Gospels (384), Psalms from the Septuagint (the ‘Gallican Psalter’) and a new Old Testament from the Hebrew (c. 390–405).
fathers/jerome/works/1/title: Preface to Samuel and Kings (Prologus Galeatus)
fathers/jerome/works/1/note: Lists the Hebrew canon and places other books ‘among the apocrypha’.
fathers/jerome/works/3/note: Argues for the superiority of virginity; criticised in Rome for disparaging marriage.
fathers/jerome/works/4/note: Biographical catalogue of 135 Christian writers, ending with himself.
fathers/jerome/works/5/note: About 120 letters, including Letter 22 to Eustochium on virginity and his exchange with Augustine.
fathers/jerome/works/6/note: Early work on the reception of Arian-baptised bishops.
fathers/jerome/doctrineContributions/0/t: Gave the West its standard Bible and the argument for translating from the original languages; his canon distinction underlies later Protestant and Catholic debates about the deuterocanonical books.
fathers/jerome/doctrineContributions/1/t: His case for Mary’s perpetual virginity and for the veneration of relics became standard in Western theology.
fathers/jerome/doctrineContributions/2/t: His ranking of virginity above marriage shaped Western attitudes to celibacy, though the Church did not adopt his harshest statements.
fathers/jerome/doctrineContributions/3/t: Introduced Latin readers to Greek and Jewish exegesis and to a philological approach to the biblical text.
fathers/jerome/laterInfluence/0/text: The Vulgate shaped the language of Western liturgy, theology and literature; his prefaces were copied in Bibles throughout the Middle Ages.
fathers/jerome/laterInfluence/1/text: Erasmus’s edition (1516) made him the patron of Christian humanism; Luther respected his learning but disliked his asceticism; the Thirty-Nine Articles (Art. VI) cite ‘Hierome’ for reading the Apocrypha ‘for example of life’ but not doctrine.
fathers/jerome/laterInfluence/2/text: Trent declared the Vulgate authentic for public use (1546); the Sixto-Clementine Vulgate (1592) and the Nova Vulgata (1979) followed.
fathers/jerome/laterInfluence/3/text: His insistence on the original languages anticipated the ad fontes principle of Renaissance and modern biblical criticism.
fathers/jerome/reception/0/text: One of the four great Latin Doctors; feast 30 September; patron of translators, librarians and biblical scholars.
fathers/jerome/reception/1/text: Commemorated on 15 June as Blessed Jerome, though his works are little read in the Greek East.
fathers/jerome/reception/2/text: Valued as a biblical scholar and for his Hebrew canon, while his asceticism, Marian views and invective are criticised.
fathers/jerome/reception/3/text: Cited in the Thirty-Nine Articles and commemorated on 30 September.
fathers/jerome/controversies/0: The quarrel with Rufinus over Origen, conducted with personal invective on both sides
fathers/jerome/controversies/1: Against Jovinian’s disparagement of marriage, which provoked criticism even from his supporters
fathers/jerome/controversies/2: His correspondence with Augustine on Peter’s rebuke at Antioch (Galatians 2) and on translating from the Hebrew rather than the Septuagint
fathers/jerome/controversies/3: His disputed birth date and the location of Stridon
fathers/jerome/quote/text: Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.
